title: Topic 2 Coastal environments - Hodder practice questions

questions.question_text: Figure 2.43 shows a coastal landform. Identify the coastal landform.

points: A stack / sea stack [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award 1 mark for stack or sea stack.

questions.question_text: Describe the main characteristics of the landform shown in Figure 2.43.

points: Tall / steep-sided / vertical pillar of rock [1]
Thinner / notched just above the base due to wave attack than at the wider base [1]
Relatively angular / flat towards the top [1]
Isolated / detached from the headland [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award up to 2 marks for descriptive characteristics of the stack shown.

questions.question_text: Explain how this landform was formed.

points: On a headland, marine erosion (hydraulic action and abrasion) exploits lines of weakness / joints / faults to create a sea cave [1]
Erosion continues and cuts through both sides of the headland to form a sea arch [1]
Weathering weakens the arch roof and wave undercutting causes the arch roof to collapse under gravity, leaving an isolated stack [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award up to 3 marks for the sequence: fault/weakness -> cave -> arch -> roof collapse leaving a stack.

questions.question_text: Figure 2.44 shows the global distribution of mangrove forests. Describe the distribution of mangrove forests as shown on the map.

points: Mangroves are largely located along tropical coastlines / between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn (23.5°N and 23.5°S) [1]
They are concentrated along the coasts of Southeast Asia, South Asia, Central America, northern South America, and parts of East and West Africa [1]
They extend into warm temperate waters / subtropics in a few places (e.g. Florida, southern Japan, Australia, New Zealand) [1]
They are absent from cold temperate and polar coastlines / west coasts of South America and Southern Africa due to cold ocean currents [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award up to 3 marks for describing global pattern, key concentrations, and limits/anomalies.

questions.question_text: Explain why mangroves occur in tidal estuaries.

points: Tidal estuaries provide sheltered waters protected from strong wave action [1]
Rivers deposit fine silt and mud, creating soft, nutrient-rich muddy sediment for roots to anchor in [1]
Intertidal zone has fluctuating brackish water (mix of fresh and salt water) to which mangrove prop roots / pneumatophores are adapted [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award up to 2 marks for explaining sheltered conditions and accumulation of mud/silt.

questions.question_text: Figure 2.45 shows part of a mangrove forest at low tide. Explain the importance of mangroves in a coastal area that you have studied.

points: Coastal protection: dense prop root systems dissipate wave energy, protecting coastlines from storm surges, tsunamis, and coastal erosion [1]
Biodiversity / nursery habitat: provides breeding and nursery grounds for commercially valuable fish, crabs, and prawns, supporting local livelihoods [1]
Ecosystem services: traps sediment to keep offshore coral reefs clear, and acts as a significant carbon sink (blue carbon) [1]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award up to 3 marks for explaining at least two distinct benefits (protection, nursery/biodiversity, sediment trapping/carbon sink).

points: Clearing for aquaculture (e.g. shrimp / prawn farming) removes large areas of mangrove swamps [1] which also contaminates surrounding waters with chemicals [1]
OR: Coastal urban development / tourism infrastructure clearing land for resorts, ports, and housing [1-2]
OR: Deforestation for timber, charcoal, and firewood [1-2]
OR: Pollution from oil spills, agricultural runoff, and plastic waste suffocating root pneumatophores [1-2]
marking_scheme.rubric: Award 1 mark for identifying the pressure, and 1 mark for developed explanation.

questions.question_text: Assess the opportunities and hazards of living in coastal areas.

inputs.label: Nhập bài làm Case Study (7 marks):

points: Opportunities: Ports and global trade routes; commercial fishing and aquaculture; tourism and recreation (hotels, beaches, watersports); fertile agricultural land on deltaic plains; renewable energy (offshore wind, tidal, wave) [1-3 marks]

Hazards: Coastal erosion destroying properties and infrastructure; coastal flooding from storm surges and tropical cyclones; sea-level rise due to climate change; tsunami risk in tectonically active zones [1-3 marks]
Named case study support: e.g. Holderness Coast (UK - erosion), Bangladesh / Maldives (coastal flooding and sea-level rise), or Southeast Asia [1-2 marks]
Assessment / Evaluation: Weighing whether opportunities outweigh hazards or how management strategies mitigate risks [1 mark]
marking_scheme.rubric: Level 1 (1-3 marks): Simple description of coastal opportunities or hazards without balance or examples. Level 2 (4-6 marks): Detailed explanation of both opportunities (tourism, fishing, trade) and hazards (erosion, flooding, storms) with some geographic examples. Level 3 (7 marks): Comprehensive and balanced assessment evaluating opportunities vs hazards, supported by named examples/case study, concluding with a clear judgement.
